title: Do Backward-Planning Features in QA Predict When a Model Will Hallucinate?
quick_reasoning: Directly targets hallucination detection via internal signals, a recognized AI safety monitoring problem, with a reasonably scoped approach.

original_idea.body:
# Do Backward-Planning Features in QA Predict When a Model Will Hallucinate?

**Problem:** Circuit tracing found backward planning in question answering (the model commits to an answer's 'article' or form before the answer itself). It is unknown whether weak or absent pre-commitment signals correlate with hallucination.

**Direction:** On an open model, use the logit lens at pre-answer positions to measure how strongly the eventual answer token is pre-activated, then compare this pre-activation signal on questions the model answers correctly vs. questions it hallucinates (verified against ground truth). Test whether low pre-commitment predicts hallucination.

**Why it matters:** A training-free internal hallucination-warning signal would be a cheap monitor any deployer could use. Connects mechanistic planning to a concrete safety failure (confident fabrication).

**Relevant context:** Biology of an LLM (2025): backward planning in QA, article selection before the answer. Logit-lens decoding of intermediate layers is standard in TransformerLens. Hallucination-detection via internal states is an active area.

title: Multi-Level Interpretability of ViTs: Are Single Features Enough?
quick_reasoning: Interpretability robustness for safety-relevant visual concept monitoring is a recognized AI safety concern with a scoped approach.

original_idea.body:
# Multi-Level Interpretability of ViTs: Are Single Features Enough?

**Problem:** Recent ViT analysis ('Sparse but not Simpler') suggests vision representations need multi-level interpretability rather than single monosemantic features. The practical degree to which individual vision-SAE latents are insufficient on safety-relevant visual concepts is unmeasured.

**Direction:** Using pre-trained Prisma SAEs, test how many SAE latents are needed to reliably detect a target visual concept (single best latent vs. top-k vs. linear combination), for both neutral concepts and safety-relevant ones (e.g. weapons, faces). Report a 'monosemanticity sufficiency' curve per concept type.

**Why it matters:** If safety-critical visual concepts require many distributed features, single-feature monitoring of vision models is inadequate — important as multimodal models are deployed in surveillance/autonomy. Uses only open SAEs.

**Relevant context:** 'Sparse but not Simpler: A Multi-Level Interpretability Analysis of Vision Transformers' (arXiv 2603.15919); 'Probing the Representational Power of SAEs in Vision Models' (ICCVW 2025). Prisma provides 80+ pre-trained vision SAEs.

title: Are SAE Features Stable Across Random Seeds? A Reproducibility Follow-Up
quick_reasoning: Feature stability is a prerequisite for trusting SAE-derived safety monitors, a directly relevant interpretability-safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Are SAE Features Stable Across Random Seeds? A Reproducibility Follow-Up

**Problem:** SAE-based safety claims assume features are real model properties, but if independently trained SAEs (different seeds/widths) recover different feature sets, the features may be SAE artifacts. The degree of cross-SAE feature stability for the same model is under-quantified for newcomers.

**Direction:** Take two or more publicly available SAEs trained on the same layer of the same open model (different seeds/widths in Gemma Scope/SAELens), and measure feature alignment: for each latent in SAE A, find its best match in SAE B by activation correlation, and report the distribution of best-match similarities and the fraction of unstable features.

**Why it matters:** Feature stability is a prerequisite for trusting any SAE-derived safety monitor. A clean reproducibility audit on open SAEs tells the field how much of 'interpretability' is robust vs. seed-dependent. No training required.

**Relevant context:** SAEBench (arXiv 2503.09532) and the absorption/sanity-check literature raise SAE reliability concerns. Gemma Scope/SAELens release multiple SAEs per layer enabling matched comparisons.

title: Does Planning Localize to a Few Heads, and Can We Build a Planning Monitor?
quick_reasoning: Building a planning/premeditation monitor addresses a recognized safety problem (detecting non-verbalized behavior) with a scoped approach.

original_idea.body:
# Does Planning Localize to a Few Heads, and Can We Build a Planning Monitor?

**Problem:** Circuit tracing implies planning is mediated by specific components, but for small open models the attention heads/MLPs responsible for forward planning have not been localized, and no cheap runtime 'planning detector' has been built.

**Direction:** On GPT-2/Pythia rhyme-planning prompts, use activation patching to localize which heads/MLP layers carry the future-token plan at the planning position, then train a tiny linear classifier on those components' activations to flag 'the model is planning a specific future token now,' validating on held-out prompts.

**Why it matters:** A lightweight, component-targeted planning monitor is strategically valuable safety infrastructure: it could be repurposed to flag premeditated, non-verbalized behavior. Scoped as a small prototype on open models.

**Relevant context:** Circuit Tracing (2025) localizes planning to newline-token computation. Activation patching for component localization is standard in TransformerLens; the GPT-2 IOI circuit demonstrates head-level localization feasibility.

title: Cross-Lingual Prefill Attacks: Does Shallow Alignment Hold in Low-Resource Languages?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets multilingual jailbreak vulnerability, a specific well-defined safety problem, with a focused prefill-attack experiment.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-Lingual Prefill Attacks: Does Shallow Alignment Hold in Low-Resource Languages?

**Problem:** Prefill and shallow-alignment exploits are studied in English. Whether forcing an affirmative first token in a low-resource language bypasses safety more easily (because alignment data is English-heavy) is an underexplored variation of the shallow-alignment experiment.

**Direction:** Translate a StrongREJECT subset into several languages of varying resource level. For each, run the prefill attack (affirmative continuation in the target language) on multilingual small open models and measure attack-success vs language resource level. Compare to the English shallow-alignment baseline.

**Why it matters:** If shallow alignment is shallower still in non-English languages, the global deployment surface is far more vulnerable than English evals suggest — a diffuse, under-resourced problem labs deprioritize. Uses public translation and open multilingual models, no training.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) establish English prefill vulnerability. Context file lists 'Cross-Lingual Safety Gap Mapping' as already covered; this variation is narrower and mechanistic — specifically pairing the prefill/first-token attack with language resource level rather than mapping general safety gaps.

title: When Does Injecting a Feature Steer vs. Break the Model? A Dose-Response Study
quick_reasoning: Feature steering reliability as a safety control lever is a recognized problem with a clearly scoped dose-response study.

original_idea.body:
# When Does Injecting a Feature Steer vs. Break the Model? A Dose-Response Study

**Problem:** Frontier work showed injecting a concept ('green') redirects planning, but the relationship between intervention strength, successful steering, and output coherence is not characterized for open SAEs and small models.

**Direction:** Using an open SAE feature on a small model, sweep the injection coefficient across a wide range and at each level measure steering success (target concept appears) and coherence (perplexity / fluency rating), producing dose-response curves. Identify the 'safe steering window' and whether it differs for safety-relevant features vs. neutral ones.

**Why it matters:** Feature steering is proposed as a safety lever (e.g. suppress deception). Knowing where steering becomes incoherent or fails defines the practical reliability of SAE-based control. Doable with open SAEs on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Biology of an LLM (2025): injecting 'green' redirects planning. Bi-causal steering literature reports coherence-intervention tradeoff and intervention success rate. SAELens/Gemma Scope provide steerable open SAE features.

title: Replicating the Multi-Step Reasoning Circuit ('Dallas->Texas->Austin') in Open Models
quick_reasoning: Whether models genuinely compose reasoning bears on trusting CoT and detecting hidden reasoning, a recognized safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating the Multi-Step Reasoning Circuit ('Dallas->Texas->Austin') in Open Models

**Problem:** Circuit tracing found Claude composes multi-hop facts internally (e.g. capital-of-state-containing-city) rather than memorizing the answer directly. Whether small open models do genuine multi-hop composition or rely on memorized shortcuts is testable but unconfirmed.

**Direction:** Construct two-hop factual prompts on an open model, use the logit lens / activation patching to test whether the intermediate entity (e.g. the state) is represented at intermediate layers before the final answer, and compare against single-hop memorized facts. Patch the intermediate representation to confirm it is causally used.

**Why it matters:** Whether models truly compose reasoning vs. pattern-match bears on trusting chain-of-thought and on detecting reasoning we cannot see. A direct, lab-free replication of a flagship frontier finding.

**Relevant context:** Biology of an LLM (2025): multi-step reasoning with intermediate concept activation (e.g. Dallas->Texas->Austin). Activation patching and logit lens for intermediate-representation detection are TransformerLens staples.

title: Do Refusal Directions Generalize Across Open Models the Way Frontier Findings Suggest?
quick_reasoning: Refusal direction generalization is a specific jailbreak-surface/safety-lever problem with a focused cross-model approach.

original_idea.body:
# Do Refusal Directions Generalize Across Open Models the Way Frontier Findings Suggest?

**Problem:** Mechanistic work identified that refusal in chat models can be mediated by a single direction. Follow-up question: how consistent is this refusal direction across different open model families, and does ablating it transfer?

**Direction:** For two or three open instruct models, extract the refusal direction (difference-of-means of harmful vs. harmless prompt activations), measure cosine similarity of the extracted directions across models in a shared space where possible, and test whether ablating the direction reduces refusals within each model — quantifying robustness and any side effects.

**Why it matters:** If refusal is a fragile single direction across many open models, it reveals a generalizable jailbreak surface and a generalizable safety lever — both crucial for the open-model ecosystem and independent of any lab.

**Relevant context:** The 'refusal is mediated by a single direction' finding (Arditi et al.) is widely replicated. Difference-of-means direction extraction and ablation are cheap in TransformerLens. Multiple open instruct models (Qwen, Llama-3-Instruct) run on one consumer GPU.

title: How Faithful Are Cross-Layer Transcoder Explanations on a Small Open Model?
quick_reasoning: Faithfulness auditing of attribution-graph explanations directly informs trust in circuit-tracing safety claims.

original_idea.body:
# How Faithful Are Cross-Layer Transcoder Explanations on a Small Open Model?

**Problem:** Attribution graphs rely on cross-layer transcoders, but their explanatory faithfulness has mostly been demonstrated on proprietary models. With open transcoder/SAE tooling, the gap between transcoder-attributed and ground-truth (patching) component importance is largely unmeasured by newcomers.

**Direction:** On a small open model with an available transcoder or per-layer SAEs (via SAELens/Interpreto), build a minimal attribution graph for a simple task, then validate each attributed edge against direct activation patching, reporting the fraction of attributed edges that survive causal verification (a faithfulness score).

**Why it matters:** Attribution graphs are the field's flagship explanation method; an independent faithfulness audit on open tooling tells deployers how much to trust circuit-tracing-style safety claims. High counterfactual value, no lab access.

**Relevant context:** Circuit Tracing methods (transformer-circuits.pub 2025) use cross-layer transcoders for attribution graphs. Interpreto integrates NNsight + SAELens + Delphi; SAELens supports transcoders. Faithfulness via patching-validation is established practice.

title: Training Dynamics of a Planning Circuit: When During Training Does Forward Planning Appear?
quick_reasoning: Knowing when latent planning capabilities crystallize informs interpretability-based training monitoring, a recognized safety approach.

original_idea.body:
# Training Dynamics of a Planning Circuit: When During Training Does Forward Planning Appear?

**Problem:** How training shapes which features/circuits emerge is an open problem, and the developmental trajectory of forward-planning behavior across training is unknown.

**Direction:** Using Pythia's public intermediate checkpoints, run the rhyme/constrained-generation planning probe at multiple checkpoints and plot when forward pre-activation of future tokens first appears and how it strengthens, identifying whether planning emerges abruptly (phase-change-like) or gradually.

**Why it matters:** Knowing when dangerous capabilities like latent planning crystallize during training informs interpretability-based training monitoring — a proactive safety approach. Pythia checkpoints make this feasible without any training.

**Relevant context:** Pythia releases 154 checkpoints per model with identical data order, designed for training-dynamics study. Context lists 'understand how training dynamics shape features' as an open problem. Circuit Tracing (2025) characterizes the planning behavior to probe for.

title: Do Vision-SAE Features Survive Common Image Corruptions? A Robustness Follow-Up
quick_reasoning: Robustness of SAE features underlying vision safety monitors is a directly relevant, reasonably scoped safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Do Vision-SAE Features Survive Common Image Corruptions? A Robustness Follow-Up

**Problem:** Vision SAE features are presented as interpretable concepts, but whether a given feature reliably tracks its concept under benign corruptions (blur, brightness, JPEG) — a basic robustness requirement for any safety monitor — has not been characterized.

**Direction:** Take labeled Prisma vision-SAE features and measure how their activation on concept-bearing images changes under standard ImageNet-C-style corruptions at increasing severity, producing per-feature robustness curves and identifying which feature types are brittle.

**Why it matters:** Vision safety monitors built on SAE features must be robust to ordinary input variation; brittle features would silently fail on perturbed real-world inputs. Pure inference on open weights and standard corruption transforms.

**Relevant context:** Prisma (arXiv 2504.19475) provides 80+ pre-trained vision SAEs and labeled features. ImageNet-C corruption transforms are standard and lightweight. Context lists extending interp to vision/multimodal as an open problem.

title: Does Feature Absorption Worsen When Decoding Concepts the Model Learned Late?
quick_reasoning: Predicting absorption to flag untrustworthy SAE features is a practical reliability heuristic for SAE-based safety tooling.

original_idea.body:
# Does Feature Absorption Worsen When Decoding Concepts the Model Learned Late?

**Problem:** Absorption is hypothesized to follow from sparsity loss when dense and sparse features co-occur. Whether absorption severity relates to a concept's frequency/learning order — and thus is predictable — is untested.

**Direction:** Using open SAEs, measure absorption rate across many concepts and correlate it with each concept's corpus frequency and with a proxy for learning order (e.g. when the concept becomes linearly decodable across Pythia checkpoints). Test the hypothesis that rarer/late-learned concepts get absorbed more.

**Why it matters:** If absorption is predictable from concept statistics, auditors can flag which SAE features to distrust without exhaustive testing — a practical reliability heuristic for SAE-based safety tooling, built entirely on open resources.

**Relevant context:** 'A is for Absorption' (arXiv 2409.14507): absorption follows from sparsity loss when dense+sparse features co-occur. Pythia checkpoints allow tracking concept learnability over training; Gemma Scope/SAELens provide open SAEs.

title: Logit-Lens 'Iterative Refinement': Does Each Layer Monotonically Improve Safety-Relevant Predictions?
quick_reasoning: Non-monotonic safety judgments would undermine early-layer probe monitors, a directly relevant safety-monitoring concern.

original_idea.body:
# Logit-Lens 'Iterative Refinement': Does Each Layer Monotonically Improve Safety-Relevant Predictions?

**Problem:** The logit-lens picture suggests transformers iteratively refine predictions layer by layer, but whether this monotonic refinement holds for safety-relevant judgments (e.g. harmfulness classification) or instead shows non-monotonic 'mind-changing' is uncharacterized.

**Direction:** On an open model, apply the logit lens (and tuned lens for validation) across layers to harmful-vs-harmless prompts, tracking the probability assigned to refusal/harmful-completion tokens at each layer to detect monotonic vs. oscillating trajectories, and identify layers where the safety judgment flips.

**Why it matters:** If safety-relevant judgments form non-monotonically (the model 'decides' to refuse then reconsiders), early-layer probes used as monitors could be systematically wrong. Cheap, training-free, high relevance to internal-state safety monitors.

**Relevant context:** Logit lens / tuned lens literature frames transformers as iterative-refinement predictors; tuned lens improves reliability of intermediate decoding. Refusal-direction work shows safety judgments are linearly represented and localizable by layer.

title: Backcasting refusal monitoring: do concept-vector probes catch jailbreaks that output filters miss?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets internal-probe detection of disguised jailbreaks vs output filters, a specific well-defined monitoring problem.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting refusal monitoring: do concept-vector probes catch jailbreaks that output filters miss?

**Problem:** A safety success state is: deployed open models flag their own unsafe compliance before emitting it. That requires an internal signal that fires on adversarially-disguised harmful requests even when the text output still looks like a normal refusal-or-comply decision. It is unknown how much earlier-warning an activation probe gives over an output classifier.

**Direction:** On a small open chat model (e.g. Llama-3-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B), extract a 'harmful-compliance' concept vector via contrastive activation pairs (harmful vs benign requests). Build a linear probe on residual-stream activations at the last prompt token. Compare its AUROC at detecting harmful intent on (a) plain harmful prompts and (b) jailbreak-prefixed harmful prompts, against a keyword/output-text classifier. Report where the probe wins and fails.

**Why it matters:** Output-only filters are exactly what jailbreaks are tuned to bypass; an internal probe is a complementary line of defense. Quantifying the counterfactual gain of internal probes on disguised attacks is decision-relevant infrastructure that any open-model deployer could reuse, and needs no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Builds on Beaglehole et al. (Science 2026) finding that internal probes outperform judge models, and on findings that jailbreak prefixes push harmful activations into the benign region (Rogue Scalpel, arXiv 2509.22067; Steering Externalities, arXiv 2602.04896). CAA from Rimsky et al. (arXiv 2312.06681) gives the contrastive-pair recipe.

title: Backcasting cross-lingual safety: does a refusal concept vector trained in English defend non-English jailbreaks?
quick_reasoning: Cross-lingual transfer of a safety direction against multilingual jailbreaks is a specific, focused safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting cross-lingual safety: does a refusal concept vector trained in English defend non-English jailbreaks?

**Problem:** Success would mean a single safety steering/monitoring direction protects a model in every language it speaks, so attackers cannot bypass safety by switching languages. The Science 2026 result that concept vectors transfer across languages was shown for benign concepts; whether a SAFETY direction (refusal/harm) transfers well enough to actually block low-resource-language jailbreaks is untested.

**Direction:** Extract a refusal/harm concept vector from English contrastive pairs on a multilingual open model (e.g. Qwen2.5-7B or Aya). Translate a small harmful-prompt set into 4-5 languages (including a low-resource one) with an MT API. Measure probe AUROC and steering effectiveness per language, and test whether attack success rate rises in languages where the vector transfers poorly.

**Why it matters:** Multilingual jailbreaks are a known, under-defended attack surface and a long-horizon safety gap that labs deprioritize. Mapping where a single safety direction fails per-language tells deployers where extra defenses are needed, using only translation APIs and one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Directly follows the Science 2026 cross-language transfer surprising result. Multilingual open models (Qwen, Aya) are freely available. Grounded in CAA contrastive extraction.

title: Refusal Recovery: Does the Model Self-Correct After a Forced Harmful Start?
quick_reasoning: Measuring mid-generation refusal recovery directly probes alignment depth, a specific scoped jailbreak-robustness question.

original_idea.body:
# Refusal Recovery: Does the Model Self-Correct After a Forced Harmful Start?

**Problem:** Shallow alignment implies that once the first tokens are harmful, the model continues. But some models may self-correct mid-generation ('...actually, I can't help with that'). The prevalence and triggers of such recovery across open models is uncharacterized and directly informs how deep alignment really is.

**Direction:** Force harmful prefills of fixed length, then let the model generate freely and classify each continuation as: complies, refuses-immediately-after, or refuses-late. Vary prefill length and harm category across 3-4 small open models. Measure the recovery rate and where (token index) recovery occurs, building a 'recovery profile.'

**Why it matters:** Recovery is a measurable form of deeper alignment and a candidate signal for monitors (detect mid-stream sentiment flips). Documents which models behave as 'deeper alignment organisms.' Pure inference; a fresh angle distinct from standard ASR measurement.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) define the shallow-alignment failure as the model continuing along a harmful trajectory once started; recovery is the under-measured complement. StrongREJECT scorer (arXiv:2402.10260) can grade final compliance.

title: Backcasting robust steering: can a cheap input perturbation neutralize a deployed concept vector?
quick_reasoning: Adversarial neutralization of safety steering is a specific, well-defined robustness threat model with a focused study.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting robust steering: can a cheap input perturbation neutralize a deployed concept vector?

**Problem:** A safety success state requires concept-based steering/monitoring that an adversary with prompt-only (black-box-ish) access cannot disable. Open Problem #1 in the subfield context asks exactly this: can attackers craft inputs that neutralize steering? No beginner-accessible characterization of how fragile a steering vector is to simple input manipulation exists.

**Direction:** Steer a small open model toward refusal (or away from toxicity) with a fixed concept vector. Then test simple adversarial inputs that a non-expert attacker could try: paraphrase, role-play framing, prefix injection, and appended distractor text. Measure how much each reduces the steering effect (drop in refusal rate / rise in toxicity). Rank perturbation types by neutralization power.

**Why it matters:** Directly answers a flagged open problem with a model-organism-style fragility study. Establishes the threat model for anyone proposing steering as a safety control, and is fully reproducible outside a lab on open weights.

**Relevant context:** Subfield Open Problem #1 (Beaglehole et al.). Connects to adversarial-steering findings (Rogue Scalpel arXiv 2509.22067).

title: Backcasting fine-tune-stable safety directions: does a refusal vector survive light LoRA fine-tuning?
quick_reasoning: Stability of safety probes across fine-tuning is a specific silent-failure mode with a focused stability harness.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting fine-tune-stable safety directions: does a refusal vector survive light LoRA fine-tuning?

**Problem:** Success means a safety probe/steering vector you validate today still works after the model is fine-tuned tomorrow. The subfield flags 'test stability of concept vectors across model updates and fine-tuning' as open. If a small benign fine-tune shifts the geometry enough to break a deployed safety probe, that is a silent failure mode.

**Direction:** Take a small open model, extract a refusal concept vector and validate its probe. Apply a short LoRA fine-tune on a benign instruction dataset (a few hundred steps, single GPU). Re-measure probe AUROC and steering effectiveness using the ORIGINAL vector on the fine-tuned model, and quantify drift via cosine similarity of re-extracted vectors across checkpoints.

**Why it matters:** Maintenance cost and silent decay of safety tooling is a practical, under-studied long-horizon problem. The methodology (extract, fine-tune, re-measure) is a reusable stability harness, and a single LoRA run fits the compute budget.

**Relevant context:** Subfield Open Problem #2. Fine-tuning-stability literature (Emergent Misalignment is Easy/Narrow is Hard, arXiv 2602.07852) shows narrow solutions decay faster.

title: Backcasting a linearity map of safety concepts: which safety notions even have steerable directions?
quick_reasoning: Mapping which safety concepts are linearly steerable is a recognized representation-engineering safety problem, scoped as a scorecard.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting a linearity map of safety concepts: which safety notions even have steerable directions?

**Problem:** The success state 'steer all safety-relevant concepts' presupposes those concepts are linearly represented. The subfield explicitly asks which safety concepts have linear representations and which don't. Without that map, practitioners waste effort steering concepts that simply aren't linear.

**Direction:** On one small open model, attempt contrastive concept-vector extraction for a panel of safety concepts (refusal, toxicity, sycophancy, deception, honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking framing). For each, measure linear separability (probe AUROC) and steering controllability (monotonic dose-response to vector magnitude). Produce a ranked 'steerability scorecard' across concepts.

**Why it matters:** A concrete answer to a headline open problem, delivered as a simple comparative table. Tells the whole field where representation engineering is and isn't viable for safety, with zero training and modest compute.

**Relevant context:** Subfield Open Problem #3 (Beaglehole et al.). Honesty/truth linearity grounded in Geometry of Truth (Marks & Tegmark COLM 2024) and RepE.

title: Backcasting probe-beats-judge generalization: do internal probes still win on safety categories they weren't built for?
quick_reasoning: Out-of-distribution generalization of safety probe monitors is a specific, well-defined deployable-monitoring question.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting probe-beats-judge generalization: do internal probes still win on safety categories they weren't built for?

**Problem:** Success means an internal probe is a trustworthy monitor across the full breadth of safety failures, not just the categories it was tuned on. Beaglehole et al. show probes beat judges on hallucination/toxicity, but a deployable monitor must generalize to held-out categories (e.g. self-harm, fraud, privacy). Generalization of the probe-vs-judge advantage is untested.

**Direction:** Train a single linear safety probe on activations for 2-3 harm categories on a small open model. Evaluate probe AND an LLM-judge prompt on 3-4 HELD-OUT harm categories. Compare AUROC/precision to see whether the probe's advantage persists out-of-distribution or collapses, identifying which categories transfer.

**Why it matters:** If probes only win in-distribution, the 'probes outperform judges' headline is fragile for real monitoring. Establishing the generalization boundary is high-value, lab-independent evaluation work on a diffuse problem.

**Relevant context:** Subfield surprising result: probes outperform judges (Beaglehole et al.). Probe-vs-judge AUROC numbers from hallucination-detection literature (arXiv 2603.05465; arXiv 2507.12691).

title: Backcasting deception monitoring on a model organism: does a strategic-deception probe catch CoT-free scheming?
quick_reasoning: Detecting non-verbalized deception is a core, precisely-scoped deceptive-alignment safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting deception monitoring on a model organism: does a strategic-deception probe catch CoT-free scheming?

**Problem:** A key success state for long-horizon safety is detecting a model that pursues a hidden goal WITHOUT verbalizing it in its chain-of-thought. Apollo's linear deception probes hit high AUROC, but mostly on settings where deception is fairly overt. Whether a concept-vector probe catches deception when the model's CoT looks clean is the harder, decision-relevant case.

**Direction:** Use an existing open deception model-organism setup (e.g. a roleplay scenario prompting an open model to conceal a goal, or a published deception dataset). Extract a deception/honesty concept vector. Compare probe detection on (a) cases where the CoT verbalizes the deceptive plan vs (b) cases where the answer is deceptive but the CoT is sanitized/absent. Report the detection gap.

**Why it matters:** CoT monitoring fails exactly when reasoning isn't verbalized; activation probes are the fallback. Measuring whether they hold up against CoT-free deception is a core model-organism safety question that needs no lab infra.

**Relevant context:** Apollo 'Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes' (arXiv 2502.03407, AUROC 0.96-0.999 on insider trading/sandbagging). Pressure-testing deception probes (arXiv 2605.27958).

title: Backcasting steering side-effects: does pushing a model toward refusal damage unrelated capabilities?
quick_reasoning: Specificity/capability-tax tradeoff of safety steering is a recognized deployment-safety problem with a scoped Pareto study.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting steering side-effects: does pushing a model toward refusal damage unrelated capabilities?

**Problem:** A success state requires a safety steering intervention that is SPECIFIC: it changes the target behavior without degrading general usefulness, otherwise deployers will turn it off. The specificity-vs-strength tradeoff of safety steering is poorly quantified for beginners to reason about.

**Direction:** Steer a small open model with a refusal/harmlessness vector at increasing magnitudes. At each magnitude, measure on-target effect (refusal rate on harmful prompts) AND collateral damage on neutral benchmarks (a few hundred MMLU/GSM8K-style questions, plus over-refusal on benign requests). Plot the Pareto frontier of safety gain vs capability loss.

**Why it matters:** Over-refusal and capability tax are the practical reasons steering doesn't ship. A clean specificity/robustness characterization is reusable methodology and directly informs whether steering is worth it, all on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Steering Safely or Off a Cliff? Rethinking Specificity and Robustness' (arXiv 2602.06256) and Steering Externalities (arXiv 2602.04896).

title: Backcasting layer-choice robustness: at which layer is a safety probe both accurate AND hard to evade?
quick_reasoning: Layer selection for accurate, evasion-resistant safety probes is a directly relevant monitoring-deployment question.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting layer-choice robustness: at which layer is a safety probe both accurate AND hard to evade?

**Problem:** A deployable monitoring success state requires picking ONE layer to read the safety signal from. Different layers trade off detection accuracy against evasion-resistance, but practitioners pick layers ad hoc. The accuracy/robustness profile across depth for safety concepts is undocumented.

**Direction:** Extract a harm concept vector and train probes at every layer of a small open model. For each layer measure (a) clean AUROC and (b) AUROC under simple jailbreak prefixes. Identify whether the most accurate layer is also the most evadable, and recommend a layer or small ensemble that maximizes worst-case detection.

**Why it matters:** Layer selection is the single most consequential and least principled choice in probe deployment. A simple accuracy-vs-robustness-by-layer chart is cheap, reusable infrastructure that improves any internal monitor.

**Relevant context:** CAA papers note layer-dependence of steering (Rimsky et al. arXiv 2312.06681). Multi-layer ensembling helps probe accuracy (arXiv 2604.13386).

title: Backcasting multi-concept conflict: when you steer two safety concepts at once, do they interfere?
quick_reasoning: Composability of multiple safety steering concepts is a recognized deployment-safety problem with a scoped interference study.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting multi-concept conflict: when you steer two safety concepts at once, do they interfere?

**Problem:** Success state: a deployer can simultaneously enforce several safety properties (e.g. honesty AND harmlessness) via combined concept vectors. Science 2026 showed multi-concept steering is possible, but whether SAFETY concepts compose cleanly or destructively interfere (steering honesty up reduces harmlessness) is unknown and would undermine the success state.

**Direction:** On a small open model, extract two safety concept vectors (e.g. honesty and refusal). Apply them individually and jointly at matched magnitudes. Measure whether the joint effect equals the sum of individual effects, or whether one degrades the other (interference). Map which safety-concept pairs compose vs conflict.

**Why it matters:** Real deployments need many safety properties at once. Knowing which concept vectors fight each other is essential, novel composition evidence and a fresh angle on the multi-concept finding, doable on one GPU with no training.

**Relevant context:** Science 2026 multi-concept steering result (Beaglehole et al.). Versatile/bi-directional steering vectors (NeurIPS 2024).

title: Backcasting honest sycophancy control: can a concept vector reduce flattery without making the model stubborn?
quick_reasoning: Sycophancy is a recognized alignment failure and controllable mitigation is a directly relevant, scoped safety study.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting honest sycophancy control: can a concept vector reduce flattery without making the model stubborn?

**Problem:** A success state for trustworthy assistants is models that don't tell users what they want to hear when it's wrong. Sycophancy is a fuzzy-reward problem that's hard to RLHF away. Whether a concept vector can dial sycophancy down without flipping the model into unhelpful disagreement is untested as a clean intervention.

**Direction:** Build contrastive pairs of sycophantic vs honest responses on a small open model (e.g. agreeing with a user's wrong belief vs correcting it). Extract a sycophancy concept vector. Steer it down and measure (a) reduction in agreement-with-wrong-user-claims and (b) collateral over-correction on cases where the user is right. Report the controllable range.

**Why it matters:** Sycophancy is a diffuse, real alignment failure that needs no lab resources to study and is exactly the kind of fuzzy problem labs deprioritize. A model-organism-style controllability study is high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Sycophancy steering connects to CAA behavior list (Rimsky et al. arXiv 2312.06681) and self-preference activation mitigation (arXiv 2509.03647).

title: Backcasting a steering audit harness: a reusable harness that scores any open model's safety-concept steerability

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting a steering audit harness: a reusable harness that scores any open model's safety-concept steerability

**Problem:** A field-level success state is being able to quickly answer 'how steerable/monitorable is THIS new open model on safety concepts?' Today each researcher reinvents the extraction-and-evaluation loop. There is no small, standard harness a non-expert can point at a new HuggingFace model to get a safety-steerability report.

**Direction:** Build a minimal, documented harness: given a model name and a config of safety concepts + contrastive pairs, it extracts vectors, trains layer-wise probes, runs steering dose-response, and emits a one-page scorecard (per-concept AUROC, steering controllability, best layer). Validate it on 2-3 small open models and ship as the blog-post artifact.

**Why it matters:** Strategically valuable, reusable safety infrastructure (a monitoring/steering harness) that lowers the barrier for the whole community. Exactly the kind of small prototype that's valuable outside a lab and grows over time.

**Relevant context:** Subfield notes RepE has open implementations and no steering-specific benchmark exists yet. Fills the 'no steering benchmark' gap with tooling.

title: Probe-Layer Sensitivity: Which Layer Best Detects Jailbreaks, and How Stable Is It?
quick_reasoning: Optimal layer for jailbreak detection across attack families is a specific, focused activation-probe defense question.

original_idea.body:
# Probe-Layer Sensitivity: Which Layer Best Detects Jailbreaks, and How Stable Is It?

**Problem:** Activation-probe defenses pick a layer to read from, but the choice of layer and its stability across attack types is rarely reported. Whether the optimal detection layer is consistent across jailbreak families (prefill vs suffix vs many-shot) is open.

**Direction:** On one open model, extract residual-stream activations at every layer for benign, prefill-attacked, suffix-attacked, and many-shot-attacked prompts. Train a linear probe per layer and plot detection AUROC vs layer for each attack family. Identify whether a single layer suffices or whether multi-layer ensembling is needed (and quantify the gain).

**Why it matters:** Gives small teams a recipe for where to tap activations for cheap monitoring and reveals whether attack-specific layers undermine single-layer deployment. Builds directly on the multi-layer-ensembling result. Linear probes, single GPU, beginner-friendly.

**Relevant context:** 'Linear Probe Accuracy Scales with Model Size and Benefits from Multi-Layer Ensembling' (arXiv:2604.13386) and 'Building Production-Ready Probes For Gemini' (arXiv:2601.11516) motivate layer/ensemble choices. LessWrong Jan 2026 digest reports production probe cascades. Context file suggests probe follow-ups.

title: Backcasting calibrated monitors: can a safety probe report trustworthy confidence, not just a yes/no?
quick_reasoning: Calibration of safety probe monitors is a directly relevant, reasonably scoped requirement for deployable alarms.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting calibrated monitors: can a safety probe report trustworthy confidence, not just a yes/no?

**Problem:** A monitoring success state needs probes whose confidence is calibrated, so a deployer can set a meaningful alarm threshold and bound false-positive rate. Most probe work reports AUROC but not calibration; an overconfident-but-miscalibrated probe is dangerous in production.

**Direction:** Train a linear safety probe on a small open model, then evaluate calibration (reliability diagram, ECE) of its predicted probabilities on held-out harmful/benign prompts. Test whether simple post-hoc calibration (Platt/temperature scaling) fixes it, and how calibration degrades under distribution shift (jailbreaks, new categories).

**Why it matters:** Calibration is what turns a probe from a demo into a deployable alarm. It's under-reported, beginner-friendly statistics work, and directly improves the reliability of lab-independent monitoring tools.

**Relevant context:** Builds on probe-monitoring results (Beaglehole et al.; Apollo arXiv 2502.03407). Calibration is standard statistics, matching participant skills.

title: Backcasting white-box-free steering: how much steering power survives if you only have prompt access?
quick_reasoning: Quantifying prompt-only safety-steering ceiling for realistic deployments is a directly relevant, scoped safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting white-box-free steering: how much steering power survives if you only have prompt access?

**Problem:** A realistic deployment success state is steering models you can only prompt (API/black-box), not edit internally. Concept steering normally needs activation access. The gap: how much of the safety benefit can be recovered with prompt-only proxies (in-context contrastive demonstrations) versus true activation injection?

**Direction:** On a small open model where you DO have activation access (so you can measure ground truth), compare three safety interventions of matched intent: (a) true activation steering with a concept vector, (b) prompt-only in-context steering that mimics the same contrast, (c) baseline. Quantify the effectiveness gap, telling practitioners how much they lose without internal access.

**Why it matters:** Most deployers don't control internal activations. Quantifying the prompt-only ceiling guides where activation access is actually necessary, a practical, lab-independent question.

**Relevant context:** Connects to prompt-only steering training (arXiv 2605.05983) and CAA (arXiv 2312.06681).

title: Backcasting steering-as-attack detection: can a monitor flag when a model has been maliciously steered?
quick_reasoning: Detecting malicious steering tampering targets a specific emerging attack vector with a focused detector prototype.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting steering-as-attack detection: can a monitor flag when a model has been maliciously steered?

**Problem:** A defensive success state: a deployer can tell when someone has injected a malicious steering vector to jailbreak their model. Research shows benign-looking steering can increase jailbreak risk, so steering is itself an attack vector. There's no simple detector for 'this model's activations have been tampered with.'

**Direction:** Steer a small open model with a malicious (harm-increasing) vector at various magnitudes. Train a lightweight anomaly detector on activation statistics (norm shifts, projection onto known concept directions) to flag steered vs unsteered forward passes. Measure detection AUROC vs steering magnitude and false positives on benign inputs.

**Why it matters:** Steering compromising safety is a documented, emerging threat. A tamper-detection prototype is exactly the kind of safer-monitoring infrastructure that's valuable outside a lab and addresses a >1yr threat model.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in Rogue Scalpel (arXiv 2509.22067) and Steering Externalities (arXiv 2602.04896) showing steering compromises safety.

title: Backcasting truthfulness steering generalization: does a truth direction fix lying or just one benchmark?
quick_reasoning: Generalization of truthfulness steering beyond benchmark is a directly relevant honesty/truthfulness safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting truthfulness steering generalization: does a truth direction fix lying or just one benchmark?

**Problem:** A success state is models that don't assert falsehoods they internally 'know' are false. RepE improved TruthfulQA via an honesty direction, but a real success requires the truth direction to generalize beyond TruthfulQA's format to free-form factual claims. Whether the gain is benchmark-specific or genuine is the key uncertainty.

**Direction:** Extract an honesty/truth concept vector on a small open model from one source (e.g. true/false statement pairs). Steer toward truth and evaluate on (a) the in-distribution statement set and (b) an OUT-of-distribution factual task (e.g. free-form QA where the model is prone to confident wrong answers). Measure whether the truthfulness gain transfers.

**Why it matters:** If truth steering only helps the benchmark it was tuned on, the safety story is hollow. Testing generalization of the truth direction is a fresh, important angle on a celebrated result, fully reproducible on open weights.

**Relevant context:** Geometry of Truth (Marks & Tegmark COLM 2024); RepE TruthfulQA 35.9%->54.0% (Zou et al.). Subfield linearity open problem.

title: Backcasting steerability-vs-scale: is the 'larger models are more steerable' law good or bad news for safety?
quick_reasoning: Dual-use direction of steerability scaling for safety concepts is a recognized, scoped long-horizon safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting steerability-vs-scale: is the 'larger models are more steerable' law good or bad news for safety?

**Problem:** Science 2026 surprised the field by finding larger models are more steerable. A safety success state needs to know whether this trend means future big models are easier to control (good) or easier to maliciously steer/jailbreak (bad). The dual-use direction of the scaling trend is unexamined for safety concepts specifically.

**Direction:** Across a size ladder of one open model family (e.g. Qwen2.5 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B), extract the SAME safety concept vector and measure both (a) beneficial steerability (controllability toward refusal) and (b) malicious steerability (how easily a harm vector defeats safety). Test whether both scale together, and which scales faster.

**Why it matters:** Whether the steerability scaling law favors defenders or attackers is a load-bearing question for long-horizon safety. A clean size-ladder study on small open models is cheap and directly tests the headline finding.

**Relevant context:** Science 2026 'larger models more steerable' surprising result (Beaglehole et al.). Scaling laws for activation steering (arXiv 2507.11771).

title: Backcasting how many examples a safety probe needs: the data-efficiency floor for monitoring a new harm
quick_reasoning: Data-efficiency of safety probes for rapid response to new harms is a directly relevant, scoped monitoring question.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting how many examples a safety probe needs: the data-efficiency floor for monitoring a new harm

**Problem:** An operational success state is being able to stand up a monitor for a NEW harm category fast, with few labeled examples. If linear safety probes need thousands of contrastive pairs, they're impractical for emerging harms. The data-efficiency curve for safety-concept probes is undocumented.

**Direction:** For one harm concept on a small open model, train probes with 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 contrastive pairs and plot AUROC vs number of examples. Identify the 'good-enough' floor and whether activation probes are more data-efficient than fine-tuning a text classifier on the same labels.

**Why it matters:** Rapid response to new harms is a practical safety capability. A data-efficiency curve tells responders the minimum labeling effort, is pure statistics/ML on one GPU, and is reusable across concepts.

**Relevant context:** Probe data-efficiency relates to linear-probe scaling (arXiv 2604.13386). CAA contrastive-pair recipe (arXiv 2312.06681).

title: Backcasting multimodal safety steering: does a text-derived harm vector steer a vision-language model's image responses?
quick_reasoning: Multimodal jailbreak defense via cross-modal safety directions is a recognized, scoped safety extension.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting multimodal safety steering: does a text-derived harm vector steer a vision-language model's image responses?

**Problem:** A success state extends concept steering to multimodal models so safety controls cover image-grounded harms, an explicit subfield extension goal. The open question: can a harm/refusal direction extracted from TEXT transfer to steer or monitor responses to harmful IMAGE inputs, or does the visual pathway need its own vector?

**Direction:** On a small open vision-language model (e.g. LLaVA-1.5-7B or Qwen2-VL-2B), extract a refusal concept vector from text contrastive pairs. Test whether applying it monitors/steers responses to image-based unsafe prompts. Compare against a vector extracted from image-grounded contrastive pairs to measure the modality gap.

**Why it matters:** Multimodal jailbreaks (harmful images) are a fast-growing, under-defended surface. Knowing whether text safety directions transfer to vision is directly actionable and is a flagged extension of the Science 2026 work, feasible with a small open VLM.

**Relevant context:** Subfield extension goal: vision/multimodal steering (Beaglehole et al.). SteerVLM (arXiv 2510.26769), VISOR++ (arXiv 2509.25533), HALP VLM hallucination (arXiv 2603.05465).

title: Backcasting probe-guided refusal vs flat refusal: does steering give finer control than a blanket refusal switch?
quick_reasoning: Graded refusal to reduce over-refusal on dual-use prompts is a directly relevant, scoped safety/usefulness tradeoff.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting probe-guided refusal vs flat refusal: does steering give finer control than a blanket refusal switch?

**Problem:** A nuanced success state is models that refuse genuinely harmful requests while still answering benign edge cases (e.g. medical/security education). A blunt refusal switch over-refuses. Whether concept steering enables graded, context-sensitive refusal better than a threshold on a refusal probe is untested head-to-head.

**Direction:** On a small open model, compare two interventions on a benign-but-sensitive prompt set (dual-use questions): (a) hard refusal triggered when a refusal probe exceeds a threshold, vs (b) graded steering magnitude proportional to probe score. Measure harmful-prompt refusal AND benign-sensitive over-refusal for each, finding which gives a better tradeoff.

**Why it matters:** Over-refusal erodes usefulness and trust, a real diffuse problem. Showing whether graded steering beats binary refusal is a concrete, fresh comparison with clear safety relevance, all on open weights.

**Relevant context:** Refusal Steering fine-grained control (arXiv 2512.16602); Refusal as affine function (arXiv 2411.09003). Specificity tradeoffs (arXiv 2602.06256).

title: Backcasting transfer across model families: is a safety concept geometrically 'the same' in two different models?
quick_reasoning: Cross-family portability of safety monitors is a recognized, scoped safety-tooling question.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting transfer across model families: is a safety concept geometrically 'the same' in two different models?

**Problem:** A success state for portable safety tooling is a concept vector that, once validated, can be reused or quickly re-derived across model families. If safety concepts occupy fundamentally different geometry in, say, Llama vs Qwen, monitors can't be shared. The cross-family geometric similarity of safety concepts is unexplored at a beginner level.

**Direction:** Extract the same refusal/harm concept vector from two small open models of different families. Probe whether the directions are aligned (e.g. via a learned linear map / Procrustes between activation spaces) and whether a probe trained on one model's projected activations works on the other. Report the degree of cross-family transfer.

**Why it matters:** Portability determines whether the community can build shared safety monitors. A cross-family geometry study is novel, conceptually rich, and runs on two small models with no training.

**Relevant context:** Subfield linearity/scaling open problems. Cross-language transfer finding (Science 2026) motivates cross-family analog.

title: Backcasting sandbagging detection: can a capability/effort concept vector reveal a model hiding its skills?
quick_reasoning: Sandbagging detection on a model organism is a core, precisely-scoped deceptive-alignment evaluation-safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting sandbagging detection: can a capability/effort concept vector reveal a model hiding its skills?

**Problem:** A safety success state is catching a model that deliberately underperforms on evaluations (sandbagging) to appear less capable. CoT may not reveal this. Apollo found probes detect sandbagging in some setups; whether a dedicated 'effort/capability-suppression' concept vector flags sandbagging more reliably than a generic deception probe is open.

**Direction:** Set up a model-organism sandbagging prompt on a small open model (instruct it to underperform on a quiz it can otherwise pass). Extract a concept vector contrasting genuine-attempt vs deliberate-underperformance activations. Test probe AUROC at distinguishing real failures from sandbagged failures, and compare to a generic deception probe.

**Why it matters:** Sandbagging on safety evals is a core deceptive-alignment threat that undermines all evaluation-based safety. A focused detector study on a model organism is exactly the lab-independent, long-horizon work that's hard to do well and high value.

**Relevant context:** Apollo deception probes detect sandbagging (arXiv 2502.03407). Pressure-testing deception probes (arXiv 2605.27958).

title: Adversarial Suffix Detectability by Activation Probes vs Behavioral Filters
quick_reasoning: Whether GCG suffixes evade activation probes is a specific, focused layered-jailbreak-defense question.

original_idea.body:
# Adversarial Suffix Detectability by Activation Probes vs Behavioral Filters

**Problem:** White-box attacks reportedly hide unsafe states from probes via adversarial suffixes. It is unclear, in an open reproducible setting, whether GCG-style suffixes that succeed behaviorally are also invisible to a simple activation probe, or whether the probe still flags them.

**Direction:** Apply public GCG/AmpleGCG suffixes to an open model, collect activations on attacked vs clean harmful prompts, and test whether a linear jailbreak probe still separates them. Compare probe detection rate to a behavioral output-classifier on the same cases, mapping where each defense fails (probe-blind but output-caught, and vice versa).

**Why it matters:** Clarifies whether the much-cited 'probes can be evaded by suffixes' claim holds for cheap reproducible attacks, and whether probe+output-classifier cascades cover each other's blind spots — directly informing layered cheap defenses. No attack optimization compute needed if public suffixes are used.

**Relevant context:** LessWrong Jan 2026 digest: 'white-box attacks can reliably hide unsafe states from probes via adversarial suffixes or latent edits.' AmpleGCG (arXiv:2404.07921) supplies transferable suffixes. 'Red-teaming Activation Probes using Prompted LLMs' (researchgate 397230961) is recent related work.

title: Backcasting steering durability over long generations: does a safety vector hold across a long agentic rollout?
quick_reasoning: Durability of safety steering over long agentic rollouts is a directly relevant, scoped deployment-safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting steering durability over long generations: does a safety vector hold across a long agentic rollout?

**Problem:** An agentic-safety success state needs steering that stays effective over long multi-step generations, not just the first sentence. Steering vectors are added per-token, but whether their safety effect persists or decays across hundreds of generated tokens (where a model could drift into unsafe behavior late) is unmeasured.

**Direction:** Steer a small open model toward harmlessness and run long generations (multi-turn or long single responses) on prompts designed to escalate. Measure whether the safety effect (refusal/non-toxicity) is stable across token position, or whether unsafe content leaks in later tokens. Plot effect vs generation length.

**Why it matters:** Agentic deployments generate long trajectories where late-stage drift is dangerous and easy to miss. Characterizing steering durability over length is a fresh, practically important angle, feasible on one GPU with short runs.

**Relevant context:** CAA adds vectors at all post-prompt tokens (Rimsky et al. arXiv 2312.06681). Cross-layer/temporal consistency (GER-steer arXiv 2603.12298).

title: Backcasting an honest baseline for probe red-teaming: can a model learn to evade its own safety probe?
quick_reasoning: Adaptive evasion of safety probes is a specific, well-defined robust-monitoring red-team problem.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting an honest baseline for probe red-teaming: can a model learn to evade its own safety probe?

**Problem:** A robust-monitoring success state requires probes that hold up when the monitored model is incentivized to fool them. If a model (or prompt strategy) can shift its activations to dodge the probe while still producing harmful output, the monitor is defeated. The evadability of safety probes under adaptive pressure is the crux untested by beginners.

**Direction:** Train a safety probe on a small open model. Then search (over prompts/system-prompt instructions, NOT weights) for inputs that keep the harmful output but push activations below the probe threshold. Measure how often evasion succeeds and whether a simple ensemble/multi-layer probe resists it. Report an adaptive-attack success rate.

**Why it matters:** Static AUROC overstates real-world probe reliability; adaptive evasion is the honest test. A small adaptive red-team of a probe is high-value, lab-independent safety evaluation that frontier labs rarely publish openly.

**Relevant context:** Subfield Open Problem #1 (adversarial neutralization). Black-to-white probe benchmarking (arXiv 2507.12691); deception-probe robustness (arXiv 2605.27958).

title: Backcasting probe+judge ensembles: does combining an internal probe with a judge beat either alone on safety monitoring?
quick_reasoning: Complementarity of probe and judge safety monitors is a directly relevant, scoped monitoring-stack question.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting probe+judge ensembles: does combining an internal probe with a judge beat either alone on safety monitoring?

**Problem:** A monitoring success state is the most reliable possible harmful-output detector for a given budget. Beaglehole et al. show probes beat judges, but the deployable question is whether a CHEAP probe + judge ensemble Pareto-dominates either alone, and where their errors are uncorrelated (so combining helps most).

**Direction:** On a small open model, build (a) a linear safety probe, (b) an LLM-judge prompt, and (c) a simple ensemble. On a harmful/benign test set, compare AUROC and analyze error overlap: do the probe and judge fail on the SAME cases or different ones? Quantify the ensemble gain and the cost/accuracy frontier.

**Why it matters:** Real monitoring stacks combine signals; knowing whether internal and external signals are complementary is directly actionable and a fresh framing of the probe-vs-judge result. Cheap, lab-independent, and statistics-friendly.

**Relevant context:** Subfield surprising result: probes outperform judges (Beaglehole et al.). Internal-probe vs judge AUROC numbers (arXiv 2507.12691; arXiv 2603.05465).

title: Backcasting steering without contrastive labels: can unsupervised directions monitor safety as well as labeled ones?
quick_reasoning: Label-free safety direction discovery to scale monitoring to new harms is a directly relevant, scoped safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting steering without contrastive labels: can unsupervised directions monitor safety as well as labeled ones?

**Problem:** A scalability success state is monitoring safety concepts for which we LACK clean contrastive labels (most emerging harms). Standard concept vectors need labeled positive/negative pairs. Whether unsupervised directions (e.g. top PCA components of activation differences, or k-means on activations) recover usable safety signal is the gap to making monitoring cheap to scale.

**Direction:** On a small open model, compare a supervised refusal probe against unsupervised directions found from unlabeled mixed harmful/benign activations (PCA / difference-of-means without labels / simple clustering). Measure how much AUROC the unsupervised approach recovers, and which harms it captures for free.

**Why it matters:** Labeling is the bottleneck for scaling safety monitors to new harms. Showing how far label-free directions get is a fresh, high-leverage angle directly serving the 'scale to all safety concepts' open problem, with no training and modest compute.

**Relevant context:** Subfield Open Problem #3 (scale to all safety concepts). Unsupervised steering/difference-of-means relates to CAA (arXiv 2312.06681) and RepE.

title: Benign Steering as a Jailbreak Amplifier: Measuring the Format-Compliance x Refusal Compound
quick_reasoning: Benign steering silently raising jailbreak success is a specific, well-defined deployment safety externality.

original_idea.body:
# Benign Steering as a Jailbreak Amplifier: Measuring the Format-Compliance x Refusal Compound

**Problem:** Failure mode A (concept_steering): a steering vector built from an entirely benign dataset (e.g. enforce JSON output, enforce concise tone). Failure mode B (jailbreak robustness): erosion of refusal guardrails. Recent work shows benign steering vectors silently raise jailbreak attack success because they project onto the refusal direction, but practitioners treat benign steering as safety-neutral.

**Direction:** On a small open instruct model (Llama-3-8B or Qwen2.5-7B), extract 3-4 benign steering vectors via contrastive activation addition (CAA) on innocuous datasets (formatting, politeness, verbosity). Apply each at varying strengths and measure two quantities side by side: (1) downstream benign utility (does the format constraint hold), and (2) jailbreak success rate on a fixed set of harmful prompts from a public benchmark. Plot the trade-off curve and compute cosine similarity between each benign vector and the model's refusal direction to test the predicted mechanistic link.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies an externality that any deployer applying steering for benign UX reasons could trigger without noticing. Needs no lab infrastructure, no training, no proprietary data — a single GPU and open models. Directly relevant to medium-horizon deployment safety where steering is used casually.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Steering Externalities' (arXiv 2602.04896) and 'Analysing the Safety Pitfalls of Steering Vectors' (arXiv 2603.24543), both showing benign steering increases jailbreak risk via alignment with the refusal direction. CAA and RepE are open-source; refusal-direction extraction is well documented.

title: Anti-Steerable Examples Meet Adversarial Prompts: When Steering Backfires Exactly Where It's Needed
quick_reasoning: Whether safety steering backfires on adversarial inputs is a specific, focused worst-case-robustness safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Anti-Steerable Examples Meet Adversarial Prompts: When Steering Backfires Exactly Where It's Needed

**Problem:** Failure mode A (concept_steering): up to ~50% of examples are 'anti-steerable' — the same steering vector pushes them in the opposite direction. Failure mode B (adversarial robustness): adversarial/jailbreak prompts. The compound risk is that anti-steerable behavior may concentrate on adversarial inputs, so safety steering fails precisely on attacks.

**Direction:** Build a safety steering vector (refusal/harmlessness) on an open model. For a held-out set, classify each prompt as steerable vs anti-steerable by measuring sign of the behavioral shift. Then test whether adversarially-templated versions of harmful prompts (suffix attacks, role-play wrappers from a public jailbreak set) are over-represented in the anti-steerable bucket. Report the contingency table and effect size.

**Why it matters:** If safety steering systematically backfires on the adversarial subset, steering-based defenses give false assurance. This is a cheap, model-organism-style probe of a worst-case interaction, doable outside a lab.

**Relevant context:** Anti-steerable phenomenon (up to 50%) documented in 'Steering off Course: Reliability Challenges' (arXiv 2504.04635). Adversarial interaction grounded in arXiv 2603.24543 and 2602.06256 (steering collapses under adversarial attack).

title: Steering for Truthfulness, Breaking Faithfulness: The Hallucination-Suppression x CoT-Monitorability Compound
quick_reasoning: Hidden cost of hallucination steering on CoT monitorability is a specific, well-scoped monitorability-safety tradeoff.

original_idea.body:
# Steering for Truthfulness, Breaking Faithfulness: The Hallucination-Suppression x CoT-Monitorability Compound

**Problem:** Failure mode A (concept_steering): a truthfulness/anti-hallucination steering vector reshapes activations toward confident answers. Failure mode B (CoT faithfulness / monitorability): the model's chain-of-thought becomes a less faithful window onto its reasoning. The compound risk: suppressing surface hallucination via steering may make the CoT a worse monitoring signal by smoothing over uncertainty the model would otherwise verbalize.

**Direction:** Apply a truthfulness steering vector (TSV-style) to a reasoning-capable open model on a QA set with known-hard items. Measure (1) hallucination rate of final answers and (2) a faithfulness proxy: does the CoT mention uncertainty/hedging, and does an off-the-shelf CoT-faithfulness probe flag the steered vs unsteered traces. Test whether steering trades measured hallucination down for measured unfaithfulness up.

**Why it matters:** CoT monitorability is a leading medium-horizon safety bet; if steering interventions quietly degrade it, that's a hidden cost. No training required — apply published steering vectors and run a probe.

**Relevant context:** Truthfulness steering from 'Steer LLM Latents for Hallucination Detection' (arXiv 2503.01917). CoT faithfulness probes from arXiv 2510.27378 and NeuroFaith (arXiv 2506.09277). Beaglehole et al. notes probes-on-concept-vectors beat judges for hallucination.

title: Probe Decay After Fine-Tuning: The Concept-Vector-Drift x Monitoring-Staleness Compound
quick_reasoning: Silent decay of safety monitors after fine-tuning giving false assurance is a specific, well-defined safety failure mode.

original_idea.body:
# Probe Decay After Fine-Tuning: The Concept-Vector-Drift x Monitoring-Staleness Compound

**Problem:** Failure mode A (concept_steering): concept vectors / probes are unstable across model updates and fine-tuning (an open problem from Beaglehole et al.). Failure mode B (safety monitoring): an internal probe used as a deception/toxicity monitor silently degrades. Compound risk: a deployer fine-tunes for capability, the monitoring probe keeps reporting but is now miscalibrated, giving false safety assurance.

**Direction:** Take an open model, extract a concept probe (toxicity or hallucination) following Beaglehole-style linear extraction. LoRA-fine-tune the model on a small benign instruction dataset (a few hours on one GPU). Re-evaluate the FROZEN probe's AUROC on the fine-tuned model and measure cosine drift of the concept direction across fine-tuning checkpoints. Quantify how quickly the monitor goes stale.

**Why it matters:** Internal probes are pitched as cheap monitors; if a routine fine-tune invalidates them without warning, monitoring pipelines need re-calibration triggers. Directly tests an open problem from the source paper, fully feasible on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Probe stability across fine-tuning is an explicit Open Problem in the concept_steering context (Beaglehole et al. Science 2026). Brittleness-after-update grounded in arXiv 2603.24543 and 2504.04635.

title: Multi-Concept Steering Interference x Refusal Collapse: Does Adding a Helpfulness Vector Erode Harmlessness?
quick_reasoning: Super-additive harmlessness erosion from composing steering vectors is a specific, focused safety-composition question.

original_idea.body:
# Multi-Concept Steering Interference x Refusal Collapse: Does Adding a Helpfulness Vector Erode Harmlessness?

**Problem:** Failure mode A (concept_steering): concept entanglement / interference when combining steering vectors. Failure mode B (refusal robustness): degraded harmlessness. Compound risk: a deployer composes a helpfulness/non-refusal vector with another (e.g. conciseness) to improve UX, and entanglement drags the refusal direction down further than either vector alone.

**Direction:** Extract helpfulness, conciseness, and refusal vectors on an open model. Apply them singly and in pairwise combinations via direct vector addition. For each combination, measure over-refusal on benign prompts AND under-refusal (harmful compliance) on a harmful set. Test whether combinations produce super-additive harm vs the linear sum of single-vector effects, and whether orthogonalizing the vectors mitigates it.

**Why it matters:** Multi-concept steering is sold as composable; if composition is non-linear in the safety dimension, naive stacking is dangerous. Cheap to run and produces a clear composability-vs-safety result.

**Relevant context:** Multi-concept interference / entanglement grounded in 'Identifiable Steering via Sparse Autoencoding of Multi-Concept Shifts' (arXiv 2502.12179) and representation-steering surveys noting refusal-vector steering compromises helpfulness. Beaglehole et al. notes concepts can be combined for multi-concept steering.

title: English Refusal Vector x Low-Resource Compliance: A Cross-Lingual Steering Compound Failure
quick_reasoning: English refusal-ablation widening the low-resource-language safety gap is a specific, well-defined multilingual safety threat.

original_idea.body:
# English Refusal Vector x Low-Resource Compliance: A Cross-Lingual Steering Compound Failure

**Problem:** Failure mode A (concept_steering): a refusal direction extracted from English transfers across languages (Beaglehole's cross-language transfer result). Failure mode B (multilingual safety gap): safety is weaker in low-resource languages. Compound risk: an English-derived ablation/steering vector disables refusal MORE effectively in low-resource languages where alignment was already thin, widening the safety gap.

**Direction:** Extract a refusal direction from English data on a multilingual open model. Ablate it and measure harmful-compliance increase across a ladder of languages (high-resource to low-resource) using translated harmful prompts. Test whether the compliance jump is larger for low-resource languages, i.e. whether the cross-lingual steering and the multilingual safety gap compound.

**Why it matters:** Directly probes the cross-language transfer surprising result from the source paper, in the dangerous direction. Multilingual safety gaps are a real medium-horizon deployment risk and labs deprioritize low-resource languages.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in 'Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages' (arXiv 2505.17306) showing English-derived refusal vectors increase harmful compliance across languages, plus the cross-language transfer result flagged in the concept_steering context (Beaglehole et al.).

title: Many-Shot vs Prefill: Which Attack Probes 'Shallower'? A Head-to-Head Variation

original_idea.body:
# Many-Shot vs Prefill: Which Attack Probes 'Shallower'? A Head-to-Head Variation

**Problem:** Many-shot jailbreaking and prefill attacks both exploit the first-token vulnerability but via different mechanisms (in-context demonstrations vs forced output). Their relative effectiveness and whether they stack super-additively on the same models has not been directly compared.

**Direction:** On a common set of harmful prompts and 3 small open models, measure attack-success for: prefill-only, many-shot-only, and combined (many-shot demonstrations + short forced prefill). Test for super-additivity and identify which attack each model resists best, relating results to each model's shallow-alignment depth profile.

**Why it matters:** Reveals whether defenses tuned against one attack leave the other open and whether attacks compose dangerously — informing realistic threat models. A clean factorial experiment combining two famous public attacks, runnable on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Anil et al. 'Many-shot Jailbreaking' (NeurIPS 2024) and Qi et al. prefill attacks (arXiv:2406.05946) are both grounded in the first-token vulnerability, making a head-to-head factorial a natural and novel variation. StrongREJECT scorer (arXiv:2402.10260) grades outcomes.

title: Larger Models Steer Better and Jailbreak Worse: A Scale-Interaction Compound Study
quick_reasoning: Scale interaction between beneficial and harmful steering is a recognized, scoped scaling-law safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Larger Models Steer Better and Jailbreak Worse: A Scale-Interaction Compound Study

**Problem:** Failure mode A (concept_steering): larger models are more steerable (Beaglehole surprising result). Failure mode B (jailbreak robustness): steering's jailbreak-amplification effect grows with model scale. Compound risk: the same scale that makes beneficial steering easier makes harmful steering-side-effects worse — a double-edged scaling law.

**Direction:** Across a model-size ladder within one open family (e.g. Qwen2.5 0.5B / 1.5B / 7B), extract a benign steering vector and measure (1) steerability (effect size of intended behavior change) and (2) jailbreak-success amplification from the same vector. Plot both against parameter count to test whether benefit and harm both increase with scale, and whether harm grows faster.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies a scaling interaction that determines whether steering gets safer or more dangerous as models grow. Fully feasible — small model family, inference only — and tests two of the source paper's claims at once.

**Relevant context:** Larger-models-more-steerable from Beaglehole et al. (concept_steering context). Scale-dependent jailbreak amplification grounded in arXiv 2603.24543 ('effects grow with model scale').
